failing_part: leaves the exposure's main coefficient and its interval exactly unchanged and only flips the sign of the modifier's own coefficient and the interaction term
narrowest_regime: A modifier recoded in a model WITHOUT an exposure x modifier interaction (pure covariate): then the exposure coefficient and CI are exactly invariant.
reason: With Y = a + b*X + c*M + d*X*M, recoding M' = 1-M gives b' = b + d, c' = -c, d' = -d, a' = a + c. The exposure 'main' coefficient is the simple effect at the reference level of M, so swapping the reference level changes its value, standard error and interval (the fitted values are identical because the column space is the same, but the parameters are re-expressed). Simulation (n=500): exposure coefficient 0.536 [0.405,0.667] became 1.341 [1.196,1.486]; only without the interaction term was it invariant (0.898 both). Frisch-Waugh-Lovell gives invariance of the covariate-adjusted coefficient only when the recoded variable enters as a pure additive covariate; it is misapplied to an interaction.

citations.cite: Frisch & Waugh 1933, Econometrica 1:387-401 (partial time regressions); Lovell 1963, JASA 58:993-1010

bite_note: A researcher who trusts 'no post-lock check needed' will report an exposure coefficient that silently depends on an arbitrary spelling/level order, i.e. the effect in one stratum of the modifier, labelled as the exposure's effect. The reported exposure estimate and interval change with the coding; the interaction contrast and the stratum-specific effects are what is invariant.

failing_part: the correct survey weight is the weight of the largest sample on which any analysis variable was measured ... MEC examination weight ... even when a fasting analyte such as glucose is also analyzed
narrowest_regime: Analyses using only interview and MEC-exam variables (no fasting-subsample or other smaller-component variable): the MEC exam weight is correct there because it is the smallest component covering all variables.
reason: The NHANES Weighting Module states 'You must use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all the variables you want to include in your analysis'; with a fasting analyte (about half the examined sample) the fasting subsample weight is the correct one, and with dietary recall the dietary-day weight. Using the larger MEC weight on rows that are only the fasting subsample leaves the nonresponse and subsample-selection adjustment unaccounted for, so estimates are not weighted to the population; 'keeps the most participants' conflates precision with design validity (and complete-case analysis keeps only rows with the variable anyway). The rule is the reverse of what is claimed.

citations.cite: CDC/NCHS NHANES Tutorials, Weighting Module (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/weighting.aspx): use the weight of the smallest subpopulation including all analysis variables

bite_note: Chooses WTMEC2YR instead of WTSAF2YR (or the dietary-day weight) whenever glucose/fasting or dietary variables are combined with exam variables; this changes point estimates and standard errors in exactly the combined-component analyses the app targets.

failing_part: A gain of 0.01 on the primary metric's own scale ... is the smallest gain that matters for every task, including the mean squared error of a numeric outcome in its squared outcome units
narrowest_regime: Only where the metric happens to be of order 0.1-1 in magnitude (e.g. log loss for a roughly balanced binary outcome; Brier at a moderate event rate); not for MSE in outcome units and not for rare-event Brier.
reason: MSE scales with the square of the outcome's units: a fixed 0.01 is vacuous when MSE is ~1e4-1e6 (income in dollars, glucose in mg/dL) and larger than the whole attainable improvement when the outcome SD is ~0.1 (MSE ~0.01), so 'better' can never be declared. Brier/RPS are likewise bounded by prevalence and category count: for event risk 1% the no-skill Brier is 0.0099 < 0.01, so no model could ever clear the bar. The author's own note says it is a convention, not a cited rule; a meaningful-gain threshold must be relative to the baseline loss or outcome SD (e.g. fraction of baseline MSE / R-squared change).
bite_note: Changes the baseline verdict ('better' vs 'too small to matter'), the T1 equivalence margin delta = 0.005 and the stratification-optimism argument: with unit-dependent MSE the verdict is a function of the units the researcher happened to record, not of the data.

narrowest_regime: Column constant on every analyzed row including blanks. A column with one distinct non-blank value plus blanks is NOT constant: its present/absent pattern is usable information and should not be settled as excluded silently.
reason: A column with one value on all analyzed rows is collinear with the intercept; no estimator or learner can extract anything from it (zero within-sample variance, zero split gain, zero partial association). Excluding it changes no fitted function and avoids degenerate standardization (division by zero SD). The only caveat is that 'single value' must not be read as 'single non-missing value'.
bite_note: Including or excluding a truly constant column changes no prediction or coefficient of interest; the only effect is avoiding numerical errors and one fewer question for the user.

failing_part: values failing these tests are treated as already normalized or log-scale
narrowest_regime: Genomics lens: raw integer count matrices (RNA-seq-type) with many features reaching >=100. Metabolomics lens: unlogged positive intensities/concentrations on a raw scale. Outside those, the tests detect 'raw scale', not 'unnormalized'.
reason: The tests detect integer raw counts or an unlogged raw scale, not normalization status, so 'failing = already normalized or log-scale' does not follow. Under the genomics lens any non-integer matrix (unlogged TPM/FPKM, RSEM/tximport expected counts, raw microarray intensities, all heavy right-skewed) fails the whole-number test and is read as already normalized, so the refusal of linear families is never armed; conversely, data already scaled to [0,1] (min-max or sum-to-one) is flagged as unnormalized in the metabolomics lens (simulated: 100-fold span and median skew 1.24, flagged True), while plain log2 intensities are correctly not flagged (span 2.3, skew 0.02). The author's lognormal reasoning is right (a feature with 30% CV has skewness (e^{s2}+2)sqrt(e^{s2}-1) = 0.93), but nothing supports the 100, 1,000, 0.5 and 20-column cutoffs as the boundary of 'needs normalization'.
bite_note: Decides whether omics_scale is raised, which arms the refusal of linear families and the normalization question; a false negative (unlogged TPM/microarray, genomics lens) lets heavy-tailed, library-size-confounded features into linear families unflagged, a false positive refuses or interrupts on data already transformed.

narrowest_regime: Observational dietary exposure (habitual intake measured at or before the baseline outcome measurement). If the diet is randomized after the baseline measurement, the baseline cannot have been changed by diet and adjusting for it (ANCOVA) is the efficient, unbiased default; the 'neither alone' default would not apply.
reason: A baseline value of the outcome kind is pre-outcome and strongly predictive; when exposure precedes or shapes it, it can be a mediator or a collider-adjustment trap (Schisterman: overadjustment), while omitting it can leave confounding. For change outcomes, Glymour et al. show with DAGs that baseline adjustment can produce biased (inflated) estimates when exposure affects baseline or an unmeasured cause is shared, while the unadjusted change analysis may be unbiased in those cases; the reverse holds when baseline confounds. Bracketing with both models is therefore a defensible default.

citations.cite: Glymour MM, Weuve J, Berkman LF, Kawachi I, Robins JM. When is baseline adjustment useful in analyses of change? Am J Epidemiol 2005;162:267-278
Schisterman EF, Cole SR, Platt RW. Overadjustment bias and unnecessary adjustment in epidemiologic studies. Epidemiology 2009;20:488-495

bite_note: Changes what the researcher sees: both the baseline-adjusted and the unadjusted estimate are reported and a gap is flagged, instead of silently dropping the baseline (loss of confounding control) or silently adjusting (possible overadjustment/collider bias).

narrowest_regime: Regression-type prediction with n_plan >= 300 and moderate p (tested p = 10 and 100, n = 300). Not tested: p >> n with tiny signal, strongly imbalanced binary targets (hessian-scaled min_child_weight), very large n.
reason: The box is a narrowing of Probst et al.'s search space (eta 2^[-10,0], min_child_weight 2^[0,7], lambda 2^[-10,10], depth 1-15, subsample 0.1-1) and covers most of their tuned-default quantile ranges (e.g. lambda 0.008-29.8, min_child_weight 1.3-7, colsample_bytree 0.42-0.86, subsample 0.55-0.96); it clips the upper depth tail (their optimal default is depth 13, range 5.6-14), alpha (their optimal default is 1.1) and nrounds > 1000. In my equal-budget simulation (100 random draws each from the wide space and the box, n = 300, three data-generating processes, two seeds each, test MSE on 4,000 rows) the best configuration in the box matched or beat the best in the wide space in 5 of 6 runs (the sixth within 3%), with far better median performance, so excluding the clipped regions lost nothing.

citations.cite: Probst P, Boulesteix A-L, Bischl B. Tunability: Importance of hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms. JMLR 20(53):1-32, 2019 (Tables 1 and 3)

bite_note: A box of this kind versus a wider or slightly different one gives near-identical tuned accuracy at a fixed budget (the narrower box is only more sample-efficient); it does not change which family or model the researcher ends up with.

narrowest_regime: Substitution models with a log, spline or other nonlinear form on the donor and/or recipient; each curve point is a standardized (g-computation) contrast over rows with feasible intake (donor intake >= k), and depends on the analyzed rows' intake distribution.
reason: With f nonlinear, the individual contrast beta_D[f(D_i-k)-f(D_i)] + beta_R[f(R_i+k)-f(R_i)] depends on the person's own D_i and R_i, so there is no per-kcal coefficient; the only defined summary at k is the average of these contrasts over rows (or a contrast at a stated reference intake). An all-components coefficient difference (beta_R - beta_D) presupposes linearity in kcal and has no meaning when the components enter as logs. One unstated refinement: log and negative-intake extrapolation require restricting to rows with D_i > k.
bite_note: Changes how the curve is computed and labelled (population-average contrast at each k versus a coefficient difference or ratio); reading it as a coefficient difference would give a wrong number or none at all for logged components.

failing_part: because their missingness belongs to the upstream process, not the person, and does not exist at the moment of use
narrowest_regime: Provider fills that are data-processing artefacts (not person-level non-response), the deployed model will receive complete inputs, and the provider's imputation may have used the outcome or other rows (so treating the fills as unknown is the safe choice). Not valid where provider imputation stands in for non-response (refusal, not tested) that will recur at use.
reason: Whether the missingness 'exists at the moment of use' is a property of the deployment setting and of why the values were missing; provider imputation of item non-response (e.g. NHANES-style imputed income) reflects person-level missingness that will recur and can be informative. Sisk et al. conclude that the right handling depends on whether missing data are allowed at deployment, not that provider fills should always be reset, and that indicators are harmful only under outcome-dependent missingness. Median fill without indicator is also the weakest imputer and discards covariate-conditional information the provider's fill may carry; a sounder stated reason for re-imputing in-fold is that an unrecorded method may have used the outcome or held-out rows (leakage).

citations.cite: Sisk R, Sperrin M, Peek N, van Smeden M, Martin GP. Imputation and missing indicators for handling missing data in the development and deployment of clinical prediction models: a simulation study. Stat Methods Med Res 2023;32:1461-1477

bite_note: Decides whether provider-filled cells are kept, median-filled in each training fold, or given indicators, which changes the training matrix and the apparent held-out performance.

narrowest_regime: Prediction with a held-out later period and a baseline that predicts the development mean.
reason: Let SST_dev = sum (y - ybar_dev)^2 = SST_own + n (ybar_test - ybar_dev)^2. Then R2_own = 1 - SSE/SST_own <= 1 - SSE/SST_dev, so R2 against the period's own mean is the lower (conservative) number relative to the deployable baseline, and it is the standard definition (sklearn r2_score). The deployable baseline predicts the development mean, so its RMSE is sqrt(SST_own/n + shift^2), and comparing the model's RMSE with it is the like-for-like comparison. R2_own alone can be negative or low even when the model beats the deployable baseline, which is why the RMSE comparison is the right companion.
bite_note: For adjacent NHANES cycles the mean glucose shift is small relative to the SD (a shift of 2 mg/dL against an SD near 30 changes SST by under 1%), so the two R2 values and the two baselines agree to the second or third decimal and no decision changes.

narrowest_regime: Distance-based or model-based clustering of mixed-type tables, where a two-valued column is encoded as a category (matching distance / one-hot / k-prototypes / Gower) rather than z-scored as a continuous amount.
reason: A two-valued column has no scale information beyond its two labels (any two-valued variable is an affine copy of a 0/1 indicator), so the only 'amount' reading is a prevalence-driven scaling artefact: z-scoring a binary column weights a mismatch by 1/(p(1-p)), letting a rare indicator dominate Euclidean distance. Treating binary as nominal is the standard convention in mixed-type clustering (Gower; Hennig & Liao 2013 on the weighting choices). This is a convention, not a theorem, and the overall weight of binary columns against continuous ones still has to be set.

citations.cite: Gower JC 1971, A general coefficient of similarity and some of its properties, Biometrics 27:857-871
Hennig C, Liao TF 2013, How to find an appropriate clustering for mixed-type variables with application to socio-economic stratification, JRSS-C 62:309-369

bite_note: Changes the encoding of every binary column (matching category vs z-scored number), which changes the distances and so the clusters whenever continuous features are present.

failing_part: Each cross-validated score's standard error, and the interval for each pair of families' difference ... tell whether two models differ, in place of a rule about sample size
narrowest_regime: Stable, low-variance learners (e.g. regularized linear models) or moderate n, where the corrected resampled t is near nominal (slightly conservative); the per-score SE from fold spread is slightly too small even there.
reason: Bengio & Grandvalet prove no unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold CV exists, so a score's SE from fold spread is biased low. In my simulation (10x10 CV, two exchangeable learners so the null is true, 800 datasets) the corrected resampled t rejected 3.6-4.0% for OLS at n = 30-400 (naive paired t 55%), but for unstable learners (deep trees, n = 30-60) it rejected 8.7-12% at nominal 5% and the naive SE of a CV score was 30-35% below the true sampling SD. The interval is therefore reasonable for stable learners but cannot be said to 'tell' whether two models differ in general, nor to replace small-n caution; it also tests difference from zero, not practical equivalence.

citations.cite: Bengio Y, Grandvalet Y. No unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold cross-validation. JMLR 5:1089-1105, 2004
Nadeau C, Bengio Y. Inference for the generalization error. Machine Learning 52:239-281, 2003
Bouckaert RR, Frank E. Evaluating the replicability of significance tests for comparing learning algorithms. PAKDD 2004, LNAI 3056:3-12

bite_note: Changes family-comparison verdicts: with high-variance families at small n, 'the families differ' is declared about twice as often as nominal, which can lead a researcher to prefer a more complex family; the alternative of a naive paired t is far worse and a sample-size rule is cruder.
